Repairs are in. All three listed sheet failures came from figure-spec text that the renderer could not satisfy, so I fixed the specs rather than the invention text.

**FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 (hatching):** both briefs prescribed hatch angles and comparative steepness ("legs rising to the right", "band falling to the right more steeply than the slab", the FIG. 4 stack of three differently sloped bands). The renderer applies one hatch angle, so every comparative and directional statement was a guaranteed mismatch on inspection. Hatch slope is not disclosure-grounded geometry, so I removed the angle and direction prescriptions and kept the thing that actually separates the bodies: regularly spaced parallel hatching on each cut body with a plain solid line along every join. FIG. 4's cross-references to FIG. 2's hatch direction went with them.

**FIG. 5 (numeral 24):** numeral 24 kept landing in a rejected coordinate cluster on the narrow front strip of the band. The perimeter member is already fully identified on FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4, and FIG. 5 exists to show the flexible pulling element, so I removed numeral 24 and the canonical part name from that sheet and left the structure as an unnumbered band under the body, as context only. FIG. 5 now carries 10, 36, 46. The Brief Description of the Drawings entry for FIG. 5 was updated to match.

I edited the figure specifications and the drawings section; I did not run the image pipeline or the gates myself, so the regeneration and re-inspection happen on this turn's publish, not in anything I verified here.

input.summary: Resolved all three drawing-gate blockers from the previous QA report by correcting figure specifications, with one consequential synchronization in the Brief Description of the Drawings. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 failed semantic review because their briefs prescribed hatching directions and comparative steepness between adjacent cut bodies that the renderer does not vary; those prescriptions are drawing convention, not disclosure-grounded geometry, so they were removed and replaced with the positive statement that each cut body carries regularly spaced parallel hatching and that a plain solid line runs along every join. FIG. 5 failed leader placement on numeral 24, which repeatedly landed in a rejected coordinate cluster on the narrow front strip of the band; since the perimeter member is fully identified on FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4, numeral 24 and the canonical part name were removed from FIG. 5 and the structure left as an unnumbered band shown only as context, and the FIG. 5 sentence in the drawings section was updated accordingly. No claim, no numeral definition, and no technical statement in the specification was changed. Note on verification: the figure specifications were edited here, but the image regeneration and the geometry, leader, OCR and visual gates run in the publish pipeline, not in this session, so I have not personally observed those checks pass.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 failures were all of one kind: the brief asserted relative hatch slopes (legs rising to the right, covering element steeper than the base) that the renderer cannot honour because it applies a single hatch pattern. Any comparative or directional hatch statement in these briefs is therefore a standing semantic-review failure. Hatch angle is a depiction convention with no support in the inventor source, so the correct repair is to delete the unsatisfiable constraint rather than to keep regenerating against it.

Body separation still has to read in a sectional view, so I kept the positive, renderable requirement that carries that work: each cut body filled with regularly spaced parallel hatching, and a plain solid line along each join so adjacent bodies do not merge. This is stated affirmatively rather than as a ban on linework.

FIG. 4 carried the same defect twice, once in the three-band stack and once in the column, and both statements cross-referenced FIG. 2's hatch direction. Removing the direction language from FIG. 2 without removing those cross-references would have left the brief internally inconsistent, so both were cut in the same pass.

For FIG. 5 the leader failure was positional, not descriptive: numeral 24 targeted the front strip of a band drawn under the rectangular body, and the endpoint inspection rejected the cluster. Rather than tightening the target with an aesthetic coordinate constraint, which the drafting rules forbid, I removed the numeral from the sheet. # FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work only; the geometry carries no lettering, the numerals below being added in the annotation pass. The vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower drawing area. The machine stands on its right-hand part, with open tile to the left.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a convention for this sheet only.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width and drawn deep; its depth is schematic. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile, and an open stretch of tile lies in front of the machine.

The rectangular body is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface. The view being taken from the front left, the body's left-hand end is presented to the viewer and the body and band share one continuous outer edge on that side, while the right-hand end reads as one boundary edge only, running between the top face and the band.

The flexible pulling element 46 is drawn as one slack curved path in the manner of a loose cord, a single unbroken stroke carrying a heavy line weight, clearly heavier than the rest of the line work on this sheet, so that the path reads as a cord and not as an edge. It begins where it meets the left-hand side of the machine, that meeting place shown schematically with no attachment formation, and runs away to the left, sagging over the tile and stopping well inside the left-hand limit of the drawing area. From the machine to that stopping point it is one long, wide, gently curved sweep lying over open tile, crossing and touching no other line along the whole of that sweep.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile. Identified well inside the open stretch of tile in front of the machine, clear of the flexible pulling element 46.

reasoning: The failure was a leader/annotation defect confined to FIG. 5, so I opened only that figure brief, the numeral table and the passages that name numeral 46. Rewriting background, claims or other sheets would have destroyed passing work for nothing.

Diagnosis: numeral 46 identifies a cord, which is intrinsically a line rather than an area. The old brief told the annotator that a point touching the path from either side counted as on the part, which permits a terminal dot sitting on blank tile next to the stroke. That reads to the checker both as a missing terminal dot and as a misplaced numeral. The fix is to give the cord a visible drawn body and to require the endpoint on the stroke.

Heavy line weight is a depiction instruction about how a slack cord is drawn, not an assertion about the invention. The specification and claims continue to say only that the flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible element connected to the device; no thickness, attachment formation, length or routing entered the patent text.

I kept the meeting of the cord with the machine expressly schematic and with no attachment formation, because the disclosure does not state how the pulling element is connected. Adding a fitting, eye or bracket to make the drawing look finished would be inventing structure.

I avoided prescribing a midpoint or a fraction along the cord for the numeral endpoint. The rule is a broad target, so the instruction makes the entire clear sweep an equally correct endpoint; the only constraint is that the dot sits on the stroke, which is what distinguishes the part from the tile behind it.

The added targeting language pushed the file to 2903 characters, over the 2800 limit, so I condensed descriptive prose (band run, body edges, cord routing) rather than dropping any geometry or the requirement that all line work stands well inside the drawing area.
